client: I've been having this constant knot in my stomach about my final exams coming up. No matter how much I try to study, I keep thinking about all the material I haven't covered yet, and it makes me freeze up. Part of me wonders if talking about it will actually help when what I really need is to just study more.
therapist: It sounds like your worry about the exams is creating a lot of tension, yet I notice your voice carries a hopeful energy too. What do you think that hopeful part might be telling you about how to approach your studying differently?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know about hopeful... I guess part of me believes I could do better if I wasn't so anxious all the time. But whenever I try to study differently, my mind just keeps screaming "what if you fail?" and then I freeze up. It's frustrating because I know I'm capable, but the fear takes over.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between knowing your capability and being overwhelmed by those "what if" thoughts. Would it help to explore what happens in those moments when fear takes over, and how you might respond differently to those thoughts?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I know logically that I can handle things, but in the moment those "what ifs" feel so real and overwhelming. Like last night when I was trying to sleep, I kept imagining all the ways my presentation at work could go wrong today. Even though I've done presentations before, my mind just spirals. 

Part of me thinks talking through those moments could help, but another part worries that focusing on them will just make the anxiety worse. Have you worked with other people who felt that way? I don't want to dwell on the negative thoughts more than I already do.
therapist:
I hear how exhausting it is when your mind spirals with those "what if" scenarios, even though you have experience handling presentations. That tension between knowing you're capable yet feeling overwhelmed is completely understandable.  

Would you be open to exploring how we might acknowledge those anxious thoughts without letting them take over, perhaps by noticing when they arise and gently redirecting your focus?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying about redirecting my focus, but when I'm in the middle of a panic spiral, it feels impossible to just "notice" the thoughts and move on. My brain latches onto the worst-case scenarios like they're facts, not just possibilities. It's frustrating because part of me knows I'll probably be fine, but the anxiety feels so real in the moment.
therapist: It makes sense that in those intense moments, simply noticing the thoughts doesn't feel like enough—the anxiety can feel all-consuming. I wonder if we could explore what might help ground you when you notice that spiral starting, rather than waiting until you're in the thick of it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying about catching it earlier, but when I start feeling that spiral coming on, it's like my brain just shuts down. Even if I know I should do something to ground myself, the anxiety makes it feel impossible to think clearly in those moments. I guess I'm skeptical that I'll be able to remember or use any techniques when I'm actually in that state.
therapist:
I hear that skepticism—it makes complete sense that when your brain shuts down, even helpful techniques can feel out of reach.  

What if we tried something simple, like a physical cue (say, pressing your feet into the floor) that doesn’t require much thought, but could help create just enough space to interrupt the spiral?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
That actually sounds too simple to make a difference. When I'm spiraling, it feels like my whole body is locked up with anxiety. I don't see how pressing my feet down would stop the racing thoughts that take over.  

It's just...when things get bad, everything feels pointless, like no small action could possibly help.
therapist:
I hear how overwhelming and all-consuming those moments feel—like nothing could possibly break through. That sense of being completely locked up by anxiety sounds exhausting.  

Would you be willing to share what *has* helped, even just a little, in past moments when the spiral eased? Sometimes the smallest shifts can point us toward what might work.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, sometimes just distracting myself helps—like watching a dumb TV show or calling a friend. But then I feel guilty afterward, like I'm avoiding dealing with the real problem. And it doesn't always work anyway, especially if the anxiety is really bad.
therapist:
It sounds like you've found some things that help in the moment, but then the guilt creeps in afterward. That tension between needing relief and feeling like you "should" be handling it differently must be really tough.  

What if we reframed those distractions not as avoidance, but as giving your mind the break it needs to come back to the problem with more clarity?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I get what you're saying, but it's hard to see it that way. When I distract myself with TV or games, it feels like I'm just running away from my problems. Then the guilt hits even harder because I know I should be dealing with things head-on. 

I worry that if I start justifying my distractions as "necessary breaks," I'll just keep putting things off forever. Doesn't that make me weak for not being able to face things directly?
therapist:
It sounds like you're holding yourself to a really high standard—where even taking breaks feels like failure. That self-criticism must add so much extra weight to an already heavy situation.  

What if we explored what "dealing with things head-on" actually looks like to you? Sometimes our expectations of ourselves can be harsher than what we'd expect from anyone else.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I guess I do expect too much of myself sometimes. It's just that when I see other people handling their responsibilities so easily, I feel like I should be able to do the same. The idea of lowering my standards makes me anxious—like I'm making excuses for being lazy.  

But you're right that I'd never judge someone else this harshly for needing a break. That double standard is something I've noticed before, but I don't know how to stop it.
therapist:
It's powerful that you can recognize that double standard—that awareness is already a meaningful step. I notice your voice softens when you talk about how you'd treat others differently; does that compassion feel accessible when you think about applying it to yourself?  

What might it look like to experiment with giving yourself the same understanding you'd offer a friend in your position? Even in small ways at first.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client:
I know I should be kinder to myself, but it just feels... fake, you know? Like I'm making excuses for my mistakes. When I think about treating myself like I would a friend, part of me just scoffs and thinks "but they wouldn't have screwed up like this in the first place." 

The idea of small steps makes sense logically, but I can already feel that resistance bubbling up. What if I try and it just proves I don't deserve that kindness?
therapist:
That inner voice calling it "fake" sounds so certain—and so harsh. It must be exhausting to carry that constant skepticism about whether you deserve kindness.  

What if we approached this not as something you *should* do, but as an experiment? Not to prove anything, but to simply notice what happens when you try treating yourself like someone who's struggling, rather than someone who's failed?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
